 USDA proposal would end SNAP benefits for an estimated 6.3 million people 
 Dani Tietz 1 week ago 0 2 minutes read 
 Facebook 
 X

 Reddit

 Odnoklassniki 
 Pocket 
 The U.S. Department of Agriculture proposed tightening eligibility rules for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program on Tuesday, a change the department estimates would end food assistance for about 6.3 million people once fully implemented.
 The proposal would restrict a pathway that allows states to qualify households for SNAP based on their receipt of benefits or services funded through Temporary Assistance for Needy Families, known as TANF. It is a proposed rule, not a final change to eligibility requirements. Written public comments are due Dec. 10.
 USDA estimates that 3.2 million households — about 16.9% of participating SNAP households — would no longer receive benefits in fiscal year 2029, the first year the department expects the proposal to have its full effect. Those households would lose eligibility because their income or countable resources exceed the federal limits that would apply without the existing pathway, according to the department’s analysis.
 At issue is “broad-based categorical eligibility,” a policy that lets states use qualifying TANF-funded benefits or services to establish eligibility for SNAP under different income or asset limits. Those services can include benefits of nominal value, such as informational materials or a telephone referral service, according to the proposal.
 USDA says 46 states used broad-based categorical eligibility as of December 2025. Of those, 37 had gross income limits above the standard federal SNAP threshold, and 41 had no resource limit under their policies.
 The proposed rule would end categorical eligibility based on TANF-funded services that do not meet the federal definition of TANF “assistance.” Qualifying assistance would include cash, payments, vouchers and certain other benefits designed to meet a family’s ongoing basic needs. Some noncash support, including certain child care and transportation assistance for unemployed parents, could still qualify.
 The department also proposes removing language allowing categorical eligibility for households “authorized to receive” specified benefits, rather than actually receiving them.
 USDA projects a $44.649 billion reduction in federal SNAP benefit spending over fiscal years 2027 through 2031. It estimates state SNAP administrative costs would increase by $928.5 million over the same period, while additional household burdens would amount to an estimated $71.7 million.
 The effects would extend beyond grocery benefits because SNAP participation can establish eligibility for other nutrition programs.
 USDA estimates about 1.78 million children would lose automatic eligibility for free school meals through SNAP. That does not mean all those children would lose access to free meals: the department projects that approximately 97% would remain eligible for free or reduced-price meals based on household income, although they could need to qualify through a different process.
 About 1.66 million children would remain eligible for free meals, 93,000 would move to reduced-price meals and 28,000 would pay full price, according to the analysis. USDA also estimates that approximately 42,000 children could stop receiving Summer Electronic Benefit Transfer benefits beginning in summer 2029, including about 13,000 who would remain eligible but would not apply.
 Comments on the current proposal may be submitted through Regulations.gov or by the other methods listed in the notice, using docket number FNA-2026-0661. USDA says submitted comments, including identifying information, will be publicly available.
